chapter: The 1960s groups, Madison Avenue and film
title: The post-quintet group with Lloyd, Szabo and Stinson
summary: Asked about the gutsy blues and swing label, Hamilton says he was just playing, with Charles Lloyd, Gabor Szabo, Albert Stinson and George Bohannon.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Gladly. So now again we’re on to that very transitional and pivotal decade of your career, the 1960s and you reformed a new group and the historical record likes to reflect that as -- it’s more as they say, “adopted a gutsy blues and swing style”. So maybe you might want to comment on that and the direction of your new group and how it’s doing, its reception.
Yes, the one right after the quintet.
Okay, this is a group with Charles Lloyd, Gabor Szabo, and Albert Stinson, and George Mahana (?) was in that group. It said bluesy and what else?
“Adopted a gutsy, blues and swing style”.
Well number one, I don’t know what gutsy blues is.

That’s number one. We were just making some music, man. I was just playing. We were swinging, that’s all. You know, the beat was there, the pulse was there and tonally we were in a very musical sort of arrangements, that’s all.
Well it would seem to me perhaps this biographical entry is referring to the fact that you’ve now replaced the cello with brass.
So maybe it takes on more of a conventional timbrel presentation, jazz timbre presentation.

Well, you know, I’ll tell you something, man. I’ve always had a thing about ­ - whatever you wanted to call what I was doing is all right with me because, you know, I just consider, we’re making music, that’s all. I mean in all honesty, I can’t say we were this or we were that, you know. So it was just being myself, man, the way I felt about it. You think that’s kind of a dumb answer but it’s a fact, you know.
